# SECTION 6: INTERPRETING THE RESULTS

## What Constitutes a Good Outcome

For a client completing her first 12-week structured resistance training programme, the following strength improvements are typical, evidence-based expectations:

| Movement | Typical 12-Week Improvement (Novice Female) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Barbell back squat | 20–40% increase in estimated 1RM | Largest gains due to neural adaptation |
| Conventional deadlift | 25–45% increase in estimated 1RM | Typically the fastest-improving lift |
| Barbell bench press | 10–20% increase in estimated 1RM | Upper body gains slower than lower body |
| Barbell bent-over row | 15–25% increase in estimated 1RM | |

These ranges are wide because individual response to training varies significantly. Factors that influence the outcome include sleep quality, nutrition adherence, stress levels, and the hormonal environment — all of which are relevant for this client and all of which have been carefully managed throughout the programme.

**An important reframe for this client:** Even at the lower end of these ranges, the strength improvement represents a meaningful increase in muscle mass and GLUT-4 expression. A 20% improvement in squat strength over 12 weeks, in a client with pre-diabetic HbA1c and PCOS, is a clinically significant outcome that her endocrinologist should be informed of alongside the HbA1c retest.

## What to Do If Results Are Lower Than Expected

If her strength improvements are below the typical ranges, do not frame this as failure. Instead, investigate the likely causes:

**Under-fuelling:** If she has been in a caloric deficit throughout the programme, muscle protein synthesis will have been partially suppressed. Strength gains in a deficit are always lower than in maintenance or surplus conditions.

**Sleep disruption:** Chronic sleep below 7 hours significantly impairs strength adaptation. Review her sleep scores from the programme logs.

**Hormonal fluctuation:** If she experienced a prolonged luteal phase or significant PCOS symptom flare during the programme, training quality during those weeks will have been reduced. This is not a programming failure — it is the reality of training with an irregular hormonal cycle.

**Testing conditions:** If the test was conducted under suboptimal conditions (fatigue, poor sleep the night before, inadequate warm-up), the result underestimates her true adaptation. Note this in the records and consider a retest under better conditions.

**The baseline comparison problem:** If Week 1 loads were very conservative (as they should have been in Phase 1), the percentage improvement will appear large. If Week 1 loads were already relatively high, the percentage improvement will appear smaller. Absolute load increases are often more meaningful than percentage changes for novice clients.

| Training Goal | % of 1RM | Rep Range |
|---|---|---|

| Hypertrophy | 65–85% | 6–12 |
| Muscular endurance | 50–65% | 12–20 |
| Power | 30–60% | 1–5 (explosive) |

For this client's next cycle, a hypertrophy-focused programme using 70–80% of her tested 1RM for primary compound movements is the appropriate starting point. This gives her precise, individualised load targets rather than the RPE-based system used in this first cycle — a meaningful progression in programming sophistication that reflects her increased training experience.

# SECTION A: GUIDING PRINCIPLES AND CLINICAL FRAMEWORK

## The Client Picture

This client presents with a specific and well-defined clinical context that governs every programming decision in this document. She is not simply a 31-year-old woman who wants to lose weight and get stronger. She is a woman with a diagnosed endocrine condition, pre-diabetic metabolic markers, and an irregular hormonal cycle, whose endocrinologist has prescribed resistance training as a first-line medical intervention. Every session, every meal, every cardio decision, and every intensity choice in this programme is made in that context.

The three risks that have shaped this programme from the beginning are:

**Risk 1: Cortisol accumulation.** Women with PCOS have measurably impaired cortisol clearance and a more reactive HPA axis than women without the condition. Chronically elevated cortisol worsens insulin resistance through gluconeogenesis, stimulates adrenal androgen production, suppresses the HPO axis, and promotes visceral fat deposition. Every programming decision — session length, rest periods, intensity techniques, cardio type and frequency, caloric deficit size — has been made with cortisol management as a non-negotiable constraint.

**Risk 2: Low energy availability.** A deficit greater than 300–400 kcal/day in this client risks hypothalamic amenorrhoea, muscle catabolism, thyroid suppression, and metabolic adaptation. The nutrition plan operates at a modest deficit of 250–400 kcal/day maximum, with protein protected at all times and meal skipping explicitly prohibited.

**Risk 3: Overtraining undermining the therapeutic mechanism.** The resistance training programme is the primary medical intervention. Excessive cardio, daily HIIT, or aggressive restriction that compromises recovery from resistance training does not add to the therapeutic effect — it subtracts from it. The programme is built around protecting the quality and recoverability of resistance training sessions above all other training considerations.

## Non-Negotiable Rules: Apply Throughout All 12 Weeks

These rules apply regardless of phase, motivation level, or client request. They are not adjustable.

- Session length never exceeds 60 minutes including warm-up and cool-down
- Daily HIIT is not implemented at any point in this programme
- Caloric deficit never exceeds 400 kcal/day
- Protein never drops below 130 g/day
- Meals are never skipped, particularly breakfast and post-training meals
- No fasted training of any kind
- If energy score ≤4 or sleep score ≤4 on two consecutive days, the next session automatically drops to deload protocol
- Resting heart rate elevated more than 7 bpm above baseline triggers a session downgrade

# SECTION A: GUIDING PRINCIPLES AND CLINICAL FRAMEWORK

## The Client Picture

This client presents with a specific and well-defined clinical context that governs every programming decision in this document. She is not simply a 31-year-old woman who wants to lose weight and get stronger. She is a woman with a diagnosed endocrine condition, pre-diabetic metabolic markers, and an irregular hormonal cycle, whose endocrinologist has prescribed resistance training as a first-line medical intervention. Every session, every meal, every cardio decision, and every intensity choice in this programme is made in that context.

The three risks that have shaped this programme from the beginning are:

**Risk 1: Cortisol accumulation.** Women with PCOS have measurably impaired cortisol clearance and a more reactive HPA axis than women without the condition. Chronically elevated cortisol worsens insulin resistance through gluconeogenesis, stimulates adrenal androgen production, suppresses the HPO axis, and promotes visceral fat deposition. Every programming decision — session length, rest periods, intensity techniques, cardio type and frequency, caloric deficit size — has been made with cortisol management as a non-negotiable constraint.

**Risk 2: Low energy availability.** A deficit greater than 300–400 kcal/day in this client risks hypothalamic amenorrhoea, muscle catabolism, thyroid suppression, and metabolic adaptation. The nutrition plan operates at a modest deficit of 250–400 kcal/day maximum, with protein protected at all times and meal skipping explicitly prohibited.

**Risk 3: Overtraining undermining the therapeutic mechanism.** The resistance training programme is the primary medical intervention. Excessive cardio, daily HIIT, or aggressive restriction that compromises recovery from resistance training does not add to the therapeutic effect — it subtracts from it. The programme is built around protecting the quality and recoverability of resistance training sessions above all other training considerations.

## Non-Negotiable Rules: Apply Throughout All 12 Weeks

These rules apply regardless of phase, motivation level, or client request. They are not adjustable.

- Session length never exceeds 60 minutes including warm-up and cool-down
- Daily HIIT is not implemented at any point in this programme
- Caloric deficit never exceeds 400 kcal/day
- Protein never drops below 130 g/day
- Meals are never skipped, particularly breakfast and post-training meals
- No fasted training of any kind
- If energy score ≤4 or sleep score ≤4 on two consecutive days, the next session automatically drops to deload protocol
- Resting heart rate elevated more than 7 bpm above baseline triggers a session downgrade
- All planned deload weeks are mandatory and non-negotiable

## Symptom Tracking System

She tracks daily throughout all 12 weeks:
- Energy: 1–10
- Sleep quality: 1–10
- Any pelvic discomfort, bloating, or significant mood changes: note yes/no

Review tracking data at the start of every session. Decisions about intensity, volume, and cardio are informed by this data, not overridden by motivation or schedule.

# SECTION B: PHASE 1 — FOUNDATION

### Session Frequency: 3 days per week

### Session A — Lower Body | Week 1

3 × 12 @ RPE 5
Light kettlebell or dumbbell. Prioritise depth and bracing. Heels flat, chest up, knees tracking over toes.

**2. Romanian Deadlift (Dumbbells)**
3 × 10 @ RPE 5
Hinge at the hip, soft knee, feel the hamstring load at the bottom. Bar path stays close to the legs.

**3. Seated Leg Press or Bodyweight Split Squat**
3 × 10 each leg @ RPE 5

**4. Standing or Seated Calf Raise**
2 × 15 @ RPE 4
Controlled tempo, full range of motion.

**5. Dead Bug**
3 × 8 each side @ RPE 4
Opposite arm and leg extend simultaneously. Lower back pressed into the floor throughout. Do not allow the lower back to arch.

**Cool-down (8 minutes)**
90-second pigeon pose each side, supine spinal twist × 5 each side, diaphragmatic breathing 10 slow breaths (4 seconds in, 6 seconds out).

---

### Session B — Upper Body | Week 1

**Working Sets**

**1. Dumbbell Bench Press or Elevated Push-Up**
3 × 10 @ RPE 5

**2. Seated Cable Row or Dumbbell Bent-Over Row**
3 × 10 @ RPE 5
Drive elbows back, not hands. Pause briefly at the top of each rep.

**3. Dumbbell Shoulder Press (Seated)**
3 × 10 @ RPE 5
Neutral spine, do not hyperextend the lower back at the top.

**4. Lat Pulldown (Cable) or Assisted Pull-Up**
3 × 10 @ RPE 5
Pull to the upper chest, controlled return to full arm extension.

**5. Pallof Press**
3 × 8 each side @ RPE 4
Anti-rotation core exercise. Press directly forward, hold 2 seconds, return. Do not rotate toward the cable.

**Cool-down (8 minutes)**
Doorway chest stretch 60 seconds each side, lat stretch against rack 60 seconds each side, 10 slow diaphragmatic breaths.

**Zone 2 Cardio (post-session)**
20 minutes on bike, rower, or elliptical. RPE 4–5. Full conversation possible. Heart rate approximately 113–132 bpm.

---

### Session C — Full Body | Week 1

Hip circles × 10 each direction, inchworm walk-out × 5, lateral band walk × 10 each direction, bodyweight hinge × 10.

**Working Sets**

**1. Trap Bar Deadlift or Conventional Deadlift (Light)**
3 × 8 @ RPE 5
Establish the hinge pattern. Lats engaged before the pull. Neutral spine throughout.

**2. Dumbbell Walking Lunge**
3 × 8 each leg @ RPE 5
Controlled descent, front knee tracks over toes, torso upright.

**3. Single-Arm Dumbbell Row**
3 × 10 each side @ RPE 5

**4. Dumbbell Lateral Raise**
2 × 12 @ RPE 4

**5. Farmer's Carry**
3 × 20 metres @ RPE 5
Moderate weight. Tall posture, shoulders back and down, strong grip.

**6. Plank Hold**
3 × 20 seconds

Hip flexor stretch 60 seconds each side, thoracic foam roll 60 seconds, breathing reset 10 slow breaths.

## WEEK 4 — DELOAD | 22–28 June 2026

### This Week Is Mandatory. It Is Not Optional.

The deload is not a reward for good behaviour or a concession to fatigue. It is a programmed physiological stimulus. The adaptation from Weeks 1–3 consolidates during this week. Skipping it does not accelerate progress — it delays it.

### Deload Parameters
- Reduce all working sets by one (4 sets becomes 3, 3 sets becomes 2)
- Reduce load by 10% across all exercises
- RPE target: 5 throughout
- Three sessions still occur — do not skip sessions during deload week
- Session structure and exercise selection unchanged

### Nutrition: Deload Week
Maintain all nutrition targets. Do not reduce food intake during deload week. The body is actively recovering and adapting — protein intake is particularly important this week.

# SECTION C: PHASE 2 — PROGRESSIVE LOAD

### Phase Goals

### Session Structure: Upper/Lower Split
Four session types: A (Lower/Quad), B (Upper/Push), C (Lower/Hip), D (Upper/Pull).

### The Tiered RPE Model
Replace flat RPE targets with the following structure on all main compound lifts:

| Set | RPE | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Warm-up set 1 | 4–5 | Movement preparation |
| Warm-up set 2 | 5 | 50% working weight |
| Working Set 1 | 7 | Establish working weight |
| Working Set 2 | 8 | Primary stimulus |
| Working Set 3 | 8–9 | Peak stimulus set |
| Working Set 4 | 8 | Volume maintenance, slight back-off |
| Accessory exercises | 6–7 | Supplementary volume |

### Rest Periods: Phase 2
2–3 minutes between working sets on compound lifts. 90 seconds between accessory sets. Do not reduce rest periods to increase perceived intensity — shorter rest increases cortisol disproportionately.

### Double-Progression Rule
When she completes all working sets at the target RPE with good form, add one rep per set next session. When she completes all sets at the top of the rep range at RPE ≤7, increase load by the smallest available increment and return to the bottom of the rep range.
